issues.description: The entire Results section is based on randomly generated dummy data from Qualtrics (N=1000), not actual participant data. All statistical tests, effect sizes, p-values, and conclusions are meaningless artifacts of random number generation. The manuscript is presented as if reporting findings, including drawing substantive conclusions in the abstract ('found no empirical support for the effect of analytical reasoning' and 'Results have supported the hypothesis'), when no real data were collected. This fundamentally undermines every reported finding.
issues.quote: Method and results sections were written using randomized dataset produced by Qualtrics to simulate what these sections will look like after data collection. These will be updated following the data collection.

issues.subcategory: Abstract reports substantive conclusions from dummy data
issues.description: The abstract states substantive conclusions ('found no empirical support for the effect of analytical reasoning on the identifiable victim effect' and 'Results have supported the hypothesis that people have a lower rating of perceived impact of donation') based entirely on randomly generated data. These conclusions are scientifically meaningless and misleading to any reader.
issues.quote: We generated a dummy set of samples in the Qualtrics survey (N = 1000) and found no empirical support for the effect of analytical reasoning on the identifiable victim effect. To extend the replication, we added the "perceived impact of donation" as a factor that is believed to be linked with the identifiable victim effect. Results have supported the hypothesis that people have a lower rating of perceived impact of donation when they faced an identifiable victim or an identifiable victim provided with victim statistics.

issues.description: The study reports no real data collection. The 1000 'responses' were generated by Qualtrics randomization, meaning there are no actual participants, no real experimental manipulation, and no valid dependent variable measurements. The entire empirical basis of the paper is absent.
issues.quote: A total of 1000 responses were generated from the Qualtrics for pre-registration (Mage = 67.80, SD=30.10; 471 females and 529 males).

issues.subcategory: Implausible demographic characteristics from random data
issues.description: The dummy data produces implausible demographics: mean age of 67.80 with SD of 30.10 and an age range of 18-120. A mean age near 68 is unrealistic for an MTurk sample, and ages up to 120 are impossible. This confirms the data are randomly generated and highlights that no quality checks or realistic parameter constraints were applied.
issues.quote: Mage = 67.80, SD=30.10; 471 females and 529 males... Age range (years) | 18-120

issues.subcategory: Merging two studies with different designs
issues.description: The authors merged Studies 1 and 3 from the original article into a single experiment. Study 1 used a 2×2 design (identifiability × intervention) while Study 3 used a one-way design with three conditions (identifiable, statistical, joint) without an intervention manipulation. Combining these into a single 2×3 design fundamentally changes the experimental structure and introduces the intervention manipulation to the joint condition, which was not present in the original Study 3. This makes it difficult to directly compare results with either original study and undermines the claim of a 'close to very close replication.'
issues.quote: In this replication, we merged Studies 1 and 3 into one single experiment to study both the explicit and implicit intervention of debiasing the identifiable victim effect... The intervention of learning about the effect would also be applied to the joint condition to reveal a more comprehensive comparison between the explicit and implicit settings.

issues.subcategory: Removal of real monetary donation as DV
issues.description: The original study had participants donate real money ($5 received from a prior survey), providing an incentive-compatible measure of donation behavior. The replication uses hypothetical/imaginary donation, which is a fundamentally different dependent variable that may not capture actual donation behavior. This is a significant deviation that threatens construct validity of the DV, yet the study is classified as 'close to very close replication.'
issues.quote: Imaginary donation Participants are required to indicate how much they would donate from $0 to $5 to the corresponding victim(s) instead of donating the money to Save the Children after signing a charity request letter.

issues.description: Switching from real to hypothetical donations fundamentally changes the construct being measured. Hypothetical donation intentions are known to overestimate actual giving and may not engage the same psychological processes (e.g., loss aversion from parting with real money). This threatens the validity of any comparison with the original study's findings.
issues.quote: Imaginary donation Participants are required to indicate how much they would donate from $0 to $5 to the corresponding victim(s) instead of donating the money to Save the Children after signing a charity request letter.

issues.description: The study is classified as a 'close to very close replication' despite multiple substantial deviations: (1) merging two separate studies into one, (2) switching from real to hypothetical donations, (3) moving from lab to online, (4) removing the pre-survey compensation that funded donations, (5) adding intervention to the joint condition, and (6) changing the participant population from university students to MTurk workers. These collectively represent far more than minor deviations.
issues.quote: Replication classification | close to very close replication

issues.subcategory: Inconsistent descriptive statistics in text vs. table
issues.description: In the text describing the post-hoc test for identifiability on donation, the reported means (M=2.54 for identifiable, M=2.24 for statistical) do not match the values in Table 7. Table 7 shows identifiable victim condition means of 2.58 (intervention) and 2.50 (no intervention), and statistical victim condition means of 2.46 (intervention) and 2.01 (no intervention). The weighted averages from Table 7 would be approximately 2.54 and 2.25, which are close but the statistical victim mean is reported as 2.24 rather than approximately 2.25. While this may be a rounding issue, it highlights inconsistency.
issues.quote: participants who faced an identifiable victim (M=2.54, SD=1.76) tended to donate more than those who faced the statistical victims (M=2.24, SD=1.67)

issues.subcategory: Post-hoc test significant but effect size CI includes zero
issues.description: Table 10 reports the Identifiable VS Statistical comparison as significant (p=.049) with d=0.076, but the 95% CI for d is [-0.05, 0.20], which includes zero. While p-values and CIs can technically give slightly different signals at boundary values, this borderline result from random data is being interpreted substantively.

The abstract claims 'Results have supported the hypothesis that people have a lower rating of perceived impact of donation when they faced an identifiable victim or an identifiable victim provided with victim statistics.' However, the actual post-hoc results (Table 14) show the only significant difference is between statistical victims and the joint condition, with statistical victims having HIGHER perceived impact (M=3.12) than the joint condition (M=2.85). The identifiable victim condition showed no significant difference from either other condition. The abstract's interpretation does not match the results.
issues.quote: Results have supported the hypothesis that people have a lower rating of perceived impact of donation when they faced an identifiable victim or an identifiable victim provided with victim statistics.

issues.subcategory: Extension hypothesis direction mismatch with results
issues.description: Hypothesis 6 states 'An identifiable victim elicits higher perceived impact of donation than statistical victims,' but the post-hoc results show no significant difference between identifiable and statistical conditions (p=1.000). The only significant finding is between statistical and joint conditions, which is not what was hypothesized. Yet the authors appear to interpret this as supporting their hypothesis.
issues.quote: Hypothesis 6 (Extension): An identifiable victim elicits higher perceived impact of donation than statistical victims... Identifiable VS Statistical | 994 | 0.91 | 0.11 | 0.03 | [-0.12,0.18] | 1.000

issues.description: The manuscript lacks a Discussion section entirely. There is no interpretation of findings, no comparison with the original study's theoretical framework, no acknowledgment of limitations, and no consideration of what the results (even if from real data) would mean for the identifiable victim effect literature.

issues.subcategory: Missing exclusion criteria and attention checks
issues.description: The manuscript states 'There was no exclusion of samples in this study' but does not describe any attention checks, manipulation checks, or data quality criteria that would be applied to actual data. For an online MTurk study, this is a significant omission as data quality screening is essential.
issues.quote: There was no exclusion of samples in this study.

issues.description: The manuscript does not provide the actual items or scales used to measure the affective feelings (upset, touched, sympathetic, moral responsibility, donation appropriateness, perceived impact). Scale anchors, number of response options, and exact wording are not reported in the manuscript, only referenced via external links.

issues.subcategory: Missing reliability information for aggregated feelings
issues.description: The authors combine multiple feeling items into an 'aggregated feelings' composite but report no reliability statistics (e.g., Cronbach's alpha) or justification for aggregation. It is unclear whether these items form a coherent scale.

There is no mention of a manipulation check to verify that participants in the intervention condition actually read and understood the information about the identifiable victim effect, or that the identifiability manipulation was perceived as intended. This is especially important for an online study where participant attention may be limited.

issues.subcategory: Power analysis based on smallest effect but wrong test
issues.description: The power analysis targets d=-0.36 (intervention effect) and determines N=314 is needed. However, the study uses a 2×3 ANOVA design, and the power analysis appears to be for a simple two-group comparison (Cohen's d). The required sample size for detecting an interaction effect in a 2×3 ANOVA would differ from a simple t-test power calculation. The power analysis does not appear to account for the actual statistical test being used.
issues.quote: Given the smallest effect size regarding the effect of intervention (learning identifiable victim effect or not) on donation was found in the original study with Cohens'd = -0.36, the corresponding sample size to detect such effect was 314.

issues.description: The text references 'Table 7' for the replication classification summary, but the actual replication classification table is labeled 'Table 6.' The descriptive statistics tables are also labeled Table 7 and 8, creating confusion about which table is being referenced.
issues.quote: Table 7 summarizes the current replication as a 'close to very close replication'.

issues.description: With N=1000 and a 2×3 design (6 cells), equal allocation would yield ~167 per cell. However, Table 7 shows unequal cell sizes (159, 175, 166, 175, 159, 166), totaling 1000. While random assignment can produce unequal cells, the specific pattern (159 and 175 appearing to swap between conditions) is unusual for random data and is not explained.

Hypothesis 4 states 'Implicitly learning about the identifiable victim effect reduces donations to an identifiable victim.' However, in the original Study 3, the implicit mechanism was not about 'learning' about the effect but about jointly presenting identifiable and statistical victim information, which activates calculative thinking. The hypothesis conflates explicit learning (Study 1's mechanism) with the implicit joint-presentation mechanism (Study 3).
issues.quote: Hypothesis 4 (Interaction effect): Implicitly learning about the identifiable victim effect reduces donations to an identifiable victim
